profiles.name: Lloyd Barenblatt
profiles.identity_context: Lloyd Barenblatt was a psychology instructor at Vassar College who in June 1954 was subpoenaed by the House Un-American Activities Committee, sitting in Albany, to answer questions about Communist activity at the University of Michigan, where he had been a graduate student. He refused on First Amendment grounds, citing the principles laid down by the Hollywood Ten. He was cited for contempt of Congress, convicted in federal court in Washington, and after exhausting appeals lost 5-4 at the Supreme Court in Barenblatt v. United States, 360 U.S. 109 (1959). Justice Hugo Black wrote a sweeping dissent - joined by Chief Justice Warren and Justices Douglas and Brennan - accusing the majority of approving naked political punishment of dissenting professors. Barenblatt served six months at the Federal Correctional Institution at Lewisburg, Pennsylvania in 1961, the same year Wilkinson and Braden served their parallel HUAC contempt sentences. Vassar fired him; he never taught again.
profiles.finding: Vassar biographical file finding aid names subject; Pacifica1960 audio corroborates Vassar/HUAC identity but recording not portrait. Archive photo retrieval pending.

profiles.name: Sam Kurland
profiles.identity_context:
Sam Kurland was a needle-trades labour activist. "Samuel" is not independently documented.

A contemporary labour newspaper reported a fifteen-day sentence for disorderly conduct during a strike in 1926; the arrest, sentencing date, facility and actual time served are all unresolved.

In the 1927 fur strike he was accused of assaulting Sam Zanistomsky on April 4 and arrested on either April 5 or April 7, the sources differing. Contemporary labour papers called the case a frame-up, which is their allegation rather than an established fact. He was initially held without bail. He was convicted of second-degree assault on June 29, 1927, committed to the Tombs on July 1 while sentencing was postponed, and sentenced on October 7, 1927 to five years at Sing Sing.

He was listed as Sing Sing prisoner number 8273 by October 1928 and at Comstock by December 1929. THE SENTENCE IS IN CONFLICT: the Comstock directory describes a one-to-ten-year term against the contemporary report of five years, and the precise legal sentence should be treated as unsettled.

His release, discharge or parole, actual time served, appeal history and vital dates are unresolved.
